steps.title: Nesting structures
steps.body:
Real data is rarely flat. A **list of dicts**, a **dict of lists** or a **list of lists** lets you model tables and records.

Chain **indexes** to dig in: students[0]["scores"][1] reads the second score of the first student.

steps.title: Sets and tuples
steps.body:
A **set** holds **unique** items and supports math-style operations: **|** union, **&** intersection and **-** difference.

A **tuple** is an **immutable** sequence. It is perfect for fixed groups like (x, y) and supports **unpacking**.

steps.title: Walking nested data
steps.code:
students = [
    {"name": "Ada", "scores": [90, 85]},
    {"name": "Linus", "scores": [70, 95]},
]
print(students[0]["name"])
print(students[1]["scores"][1])
for s in students:
    print(s["name"], sum(s["scores"]) / len(s["scores"]))

notes.text: A list that contains dictionaries, each with a list inside.
Index the list, then the key.
Chain three lookups: list, key, list.
Compute an average for every record.

steps.title: Set operations and tuple unpacking
steps.code:
a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {3, 4}
print(a | b)
print(a & b)
print(a - b)
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x + y)

notes.text: Union keeps every distinct item.
Intersection keeps items found in both.
Difference keeps items only in the first set.
Unpacking assigns each tuple item to a name.

steps.question: What does len({1, 1, 2}) return?
steps.explanation: A set stores each value once, so only 1 and 2 remain.

steps.question: Which statement about tuples is true?
options: They can be changed in place
steps.explanation: Tuples cannot be modified after creation, but they can be indexed and hold any type.

steps.title: Comprehensions everywhere
steps.body:
Besides lists, you can build **dicts** and **sets** in one line: {n: n * n for n in nums} and {c for c in text}.

Add an **if** clause to filter while you build.

steps.title: Lazy values with yield
steps.body:
A **generator** function uses **yield** to hand back one value at a time and pause. Values are produced **lazily**, so huge sequences use almost no memory.

An **iterator** is anything you can pass to **next()**; for loops use them behind the scenes.

steps.title: Three kinds of comprehension
steps.code:
nums = range(1, 7)
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
squares = {n: n * n for n in nums if n < 4}
letters = {c for c in "hello"}
print(evens)
print(squares)
print(sorted(letters))

notes.text: A list comprehension with a filter.
A dict comprehension maps number to square.
A set comprehension removes the duplicate l.
Sets are unordered, so sort before printing.

steps.title: Manual iteration
steps.code:
it = iter([10, 20])
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
print(next(it, "done"))

notes.text: iter() creates an iterator from a list.
The second argument of next is a default when items run out.

steps.question: What does yield do inside a function?
options: Produces a value and pauses the function
steps.explanation: yield hands back a value and remembers where the function stopped.

steps.question: What do the two prints show?
steps.code:
g = (n for n in range(3))
print(list(g))
print(list(g))
steps.explanation: A generator is used up after one pass, so the second list is empty.

steps.title: Flexible arguments
steps.body:
**\*args** gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple and **\*\*kwargs** gathers extra keyword arguments into a dict.

The same stars **unpack** a list or dict when calling a function.

steps.title: Decorators
steps.body:
A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns a new one. Writing **@name** above a def is shorthand for func = name(func).

Use **functools.wraps** to keep the original name and docs.

steps.title: args and kwargs
steps.code:
def show(*args, **kwargs):
    print(args)
    print(kwargs)

show(1, 2, a=3)
nums = [4, 5]
opts = {"sep": "-"}
print(*nums, **opts)

notes.text: args is a tuple of the positional values.
kwargs is a dict of the keyword values.
The stars unpack the list and the dict into the call.

steps.explanation: The decorator is called with the function and its return value replaces the name.

steps.title: Handling errors
steps.body:
Wrap risky code in **try** and catch problems with **except**. Add **else** for code that runs when nothing failed and **finally** for cleanup that must always run.

Use **raise** to signal your own errors, often with a custom exception class.

steps.title: The with statement
steps.body:
A **context manager** sets something up and always tears it down, even after errors. **with open(path) as f** is the classic example.

Build your own with **__enter__** and **__exit__**, or the **@contextmanager** decorator.

steps.title: try, except, else, finally

notes.text: Catches only the error we expect.
Runs only when no exception occurred.
finally always runs, before the value is returned.

steps.title: Classes and objects
steps.body: A **class** is a blueprint. **__init__** sets up each new object and **self** refers to the object itself. Functions inside a class are **methods**.

steps.title: Inheritance and dataclasses
steps.body:
A subclass inherits everything from its parent and can **override** methods. Call the parent with **super()**.

The **@dataclass** decorator writes **__init__**, **__repr__** and **__eq__** for you from the annotated fields.

steps.title: A simple class

notes.text: __init__ runs when you create a Dog.
Store data on the object with self.
Creating and using an object in one line.

notes.text: Cat inherits from Animal.

steps.title: Dataclasses
steps.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int = 0

p = Point(3)
print(p)
print(p == Point(3, 0))

notes.text: The decorator generates the boilerplate.
y has a default value.
The generated repr shows every field.
The generated eq compares field values.

steps.question: What does @dataclass generate automatically?
steps.explanation: It writes the common special methods from your annotated fields.

steps.title: Reading and writing files
steps.body:
**open(path, mode)** returns a file object. Modes include **r** read, **w** write and **a** append. Always use **with** so the file closes automatically.

On a phone, write to a **temporary folder** such as tempfile.gettempdir().

steps.title: JSON and CSV
steps.body:
The **json** module converts between Python data and text: **dumps** and **loads**. The **csv** module reads rows, and **DictReader** turns each row into a dict keyed by the header.

Use **io.StringIO** to practice with text that behaves like a file.

steps.title: Writing and reading a file
steps.code:
import os
import tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "demo.txt")
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write("one\ntwo\n")
with open(path) as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())
os.remove(path)

notes.text: Build a path inside the temp folder.
Mode w creates or overwrites the file.
Iterating a file yields one line at a time.
Clean up the temporary file.

steps.title: JSON round trip
steps.code:
import json

data = {"name": "Ada", "langs": ["Python", "Kotlin"]}
text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)
back = json.loads(text)
print(back["langs"][1])

notes.text: dumps turns Python data into a JSON string.
loads parses the string back into dicts and lists.

steps.title: Reading CSV
steps.code:
import csv
import io

raw = "name,age\nAda,36\nLinus,28\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw)))
print(rows[0]["name"])
print(sum(int(r["age"]) for r in rows))

notes.text: The text of a tiny CSV file.
StringIO makes it act like a file and DictReader keys each row by the header.
CSV values are strings, so convert before adding.

steps.question: Why use with open(...) as f?
steps.explanation: The with block guarantees the file is closed, even after an error.

steps.question: What does json.dumps([1, 'x']) return?
steps.explanation: dumps returns text; loads goes the other way.

examples.title: Context Manager

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tag(name):
    print(f"<{name}>")
    yield
    print(f"</{name}>")

with tag("p"):
    print("Hello")

examples.title: CSV Report
examples.code:
import csv
import io

raw = "item,qty,price\npen,4,1.5\nbook,2,12.0\ncup,3,4.0\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw)))
total = 0
for r in rows:
    cost = int(r["qty"]) * float(r["price"])
    total += cost
    print(r["item"], cost)
print("Total:", total)
